## Verdict
- Answer: CCS is technically proven but deployed at a small fraction of what climate scenarios assume. Operating capture capacity is roughly 50 Mt CO2/yr (est.), against several Gt/yr in 1.5–2°C pathways (est.). Cost, offtake and storage-permitting are the binding constraints.
- Decision: Supports selective investment or policy support for CCS in hard-to-abate sectors (cement, chemicals, some gas processing) with staged, contract-backed funding. It does not support relying on CCS to offset continued unabated fossil power at scale.
- Confidence: low-medium. All figures come from memory (est.) and no Prism calls were run. The direction is well established, but exact numbers are unverified and may be out of date.
- What would change it: Verified project-level data showing sustained capture rates, falling costs, or a large pipeline of projects reaching final investment decision.

## What the data shows
No corpus volumes, lanes, windows or news counts were measured. I ran no Prism calls, so I cannot give paper or article counts per corpus. Every figure below is an estimate from memory.

**Established (est.):**
- Operating commercial capture capacity is about 50 Mt CO2/yr globally (est.), about 0.1% of the roughly 37 Gt/yr of energy-related CO2 emissions (est.).
- Sleipner (Norway) has injected about 1 Mt/yr since 1996 (est.), with no reported leakage. Dedicated geological storage is technically demonstrated.
- Capture on gas processing and ethanol/fertilizer streams is cheapest, at about USD 15–35/t CO2 (est.), because the CO2 stream is already concentrated.
- Capture from dilute streams (power, cement) costs roughly USD 50–120/t (est.).
- Direct air capture costs far more, at roughly USD 400–1000/t today (est.).

**Contested (contested share not measurable here):**
- Whether CCS on power is worth it. Several flagship projects, including Kemper, Petra Nova (idled 2020), and Gorgon (which underperformed its capture target), fell short on cost or performance (est.). I cannot quantify what share of the literature is critical.
- The role of enhanced oil recovery (EOR), since much of the operating capacity serves EOR, which complicates net-emissions claims.
- Real capture rates (often well below the 90%+ design claim) and upstream methane leakage.
- Whether CCS delays decarbonisation by extending fossil use.
- Policy dependence: US 45Q credits (about USD 85/t for geological storage after the 2022 IRA, est.) versus carbon prices such as the EU ETS (est. EUR 60–90/t in recent years).

## Trend
Operating capacity has grown slowly in absolute terms. The figures below are rounded estimates for the approximate global operating capacity (est.), and the 2024 point is close to the Global CCS Institute's reported figure (est.).

```prism-chart
{"id":"ccs-capacity","kind":"line","title":"Approx. global operating CO2 capture capacity","unit":"Mt CO2/yr (est.)","window":{"from":"2010-01-01","to":"2024-12-31"},"x":{"field":"year","type":"temporal"},"series":[{"name":"Operating capture capacity (rounded estimate)","source":"estimate","points":[["2010",25],["2015",30],["2018",35],["2020",40],["2022",45],["2024",50]]}],"caption":"Operating capacity roughly doubled in 14 years, from about 25 to about 50 Mt/yr (est.), far below scenario needs.","supports":"Operating capacity has grown slowly in absolute terms."}
```

Quantified change: roughly +25 Mt/yr, or about 2x, over 2010–2024 (est.). I cannot supply news-volume trend series, because no news.trends call was made.

## Comparison
Baseline: current operating capacity of about 50 Mt/yr (est.).

| Measure | Value (est.) | Ratio to baseline |
|---|---|---|
| Operating capacity today | 50 Mt/yr | 1x |
| Announced pipeline (all stages) | roughly 400–500 Mt/yr | ~8–10x |
| IEA net-zero scenario, 2030 | roughly 1,000 Mt/yr | ~20x |
| IEA net-zero scenario, 2050 | roughly 6,000 Mt/yr | ~120x |

All rows are estimates from memory, and the pipeline figure is especially uncertain. Only a fraction of the pipeline has reached final investment decision, and I cannot say what fraction.

## Geography (optional)
No geo scope was given and none was measured. From memory (est.), the US leads in operating capacity, followed by Canada, Norway, China, Brazil and Qatar/UAE. The UK, Netherlands, Denmark and Norway are leading in new storage hubs (Northern Lights, Porthos, Sleipner).

## Evidence
No documents were retrieved. The entries below are recalled from memory, so verify identifiers before citing them.

- [r1] Global CCS Institute, Global Status of CCS, annual, industry/NGO, tier: grey literature. Supports: operating capacity and pipeline counts. No verbatim quote available.
- [r2] IPCC AR6 WGIII, 2022, tier: peer-reviewed assessment. Supports: CCS is needed in most mitigation pathways, with cost and deployment barriers. No verbatim quote available.
- [r3] IEA, CCUS in Clean Energy Transitions, 2020, tier: intergovernmental. Supports: scenario capture volumes and cost ranges.

## Drill-down
Layers: by capture source (gas processing, power, cement, hydrogen, DAC), by storage type (EOR vs dedicated saline), by region, and by project status (operating, construction, planned).

```prism-calls

{"id":"f1","question":"How many research papers per year address CCS, and how has the volume trended?","feature":"research.statistics","args":{"term":"carbon capture and storage"}},
{"id":"f2","question":"What does critical literature say about CCS performance gaps?","feature":"research.counter_evidence","args":{"term":"carbon capture and storage","limit":8}},
{"id":"f3","question":"How has news coverage of CCS moved year by year?","feature":"news.trends","args":{"term":"carbon capture"}},
{"id":"f4","question":"Which countries dominate CCS coverage?","feature":"news.geography","args":{"term":"carbon capture"}},
{"id":"f5","question":"How has sentiment on CCS shifted?","feature":"news.sentiment","args":{"term":"carbon capture"}},
{"id":"f6","question":"What are the key supporting studies on storage permanence?","feature":"research.evidence","args":{"term":"CO2 geological storage permanence","limit":8}},
{"id":"f7","question":"How does stance on CCS in power vs industry differ over time?","feature":"research.stance_trends","args":{"term":"carbon capture and storage"}}
]
```

## Method and limits
- **Windows:** the chart covers 2010–2024. The gap to today (2026-10-23) is about 22 months, so recent project starts and cancellations are not captured.
- **Lanes, coverage, match mode:** none applied, since no corpus was queried.
- **Counts:** no counts are presented. Every number is a rounded recollection (est.), not a measurement.
- **Censoring:** the knowledge cutoff is June 2026, and recent data are likely missing or stale.
- **Interpretation:** the verdict, the "contested" list and the decision recommendation are my judgment.
- **What the data cannot answer:** corpus volumes, the contested share of the literature, the news trend series, and any geography-scoped figure.

## References
- [r1] Global CCS Institute. Global Status of CCS (annual reports). Global CCS Institute, various years. url: globalccsinstitute.com (verify edition).
- [r2] IPCC. Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change (AR6 WGIII). IPCC, 2022. doi: 10.1017/9781009157926.
- [r3] IEA. CCUS in Clean Energy Transitions. International Energy Agency, 2020. url: iea.org.

## Verdict
- Answer: Carbon capture research is large and growing (118,216 typed papers, 2017-2025 [c1]), and its literature is mostly positive. News volume is flat to slightly down since mid-2024 [c2]. The data show interest and framing, not whether CCS works at scale or at what cost.
- Decision: Treat CCS as an actively researched field with a consistent technical base (sequestration, adsorbents, mineralization). Do not use these data to size deployment, cost or climate impact.
- Confidence: medium - the counts are solid and cover the whole corpus, but the stance split is model-assigned and may reflect publication bias [c1]. Deployment and cost data are absent.
- What would change it: Project-level operating data (tonnes stored, cost per tonne) or a critical-orientation pull that shows a larger contested share.

## What the data shows
**Volumes per corpus (lane: subject) [c1]**
- Typed research papers: 118,216, window 2017-2025 [c1].
- Papers with a real abstract, title-anchored: 1,667, window 1990-2025 [c1].
- the health literature index records: 219, window 1990-2025 [c1].
- News articles mentioning the term: 1,515, window 2019-01-01..2026-06-01 [c1].
- Patents with a matching title: 168, window 2005-2024 [c1].
- arXiv preprints: 7, window 2005-2025 [c1].

The news total of 10,735 articles in the 2024-06..2026-05 window [c2] is far larger than the 1,515 news articles in [c1] for 2019-2026. The two calls use different match scopes, and I cannot reconcile them from this data. Only compare figures within one call.

**Established (reviews) [c1]**
- Reviews cover CO2 adsorbents (164 citations [c1]), subsurface trapping mechanisms and monitoring (153 citations [c1]), carbonic anhydrase for CCUS (107 [c1]), mineral carbonation (73 [c1]), cement carbonation (67 [c1]) and basalt mineralization (57 [c1]).
- Trapping and monitoring methods, along with sorbent and mineralization routes, are well reviewed. This tells us what is studied, not what is deployed.

**Contested [c1]**
- Stance mix across 118,216 papers: supporting 74,477, qualifying 13,558, contradicting 1,169, neutral 29,012 [c1].
- Contested share (qualifying plus contradicting) is 12.5% [c1]. The brief itself notes that positive framing can mean consensus or publication bias [c1].

**Key numbers [c1]**
- Microalgae capture and sequestration efficiency ranges from 40% to 93.7% (a 2022 review, moderate strength) [c1].
- Salt precipitation in a pore-scale lab study cut porosity by about 20%, and the front moved at about 2% of CO2 superficial velocity (2013) [c1].
- A 2008 paper said a billion tonnes or more must be stored annually, a 250-fold increase over then-current levels [c1]. That figure is 18 years old and not a current deployment number.

## Trend
Research output rose from 8,225 papers in 2017 to 23,935 in 2025, a 14.3% CAGR [c1]. The late third was 2.2 times the early third [c1].


News volume fell from 482 (June 2024) to 348 (May 2026) [c2]. The late third was 0.87 times the early third, and the CAGR was -15.7% [c2]. The peak was 638 in October 2024 [c2]. Over the longer 2019-2026 window, [c1] reports a rising direction (late third is 1.91 times the early third, 316 to 605 [c1]). So the long-run trend is up and the recent trend is flat to down.

Critical coverage made up 9,166 of 10,735 articles [c2], about 85% (est. from [c2] counts). Monthly critical share ranged from 80.7% to 90.0% [c2]. The classifier's definition of "critical" is not given, so I do not read this as opposition to CCS.

## Comparison
Baseline: the earlier third of each window versus the later third, as computed by Prism.

| Series | Early third | Late third | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Research papers 2017-2025 [c1] | 26,000 [c1] | 57,283 [c1] | 2.2 [c1] |

Research is growing faster than news coverage. The two news rows come from different calls and windows and should not be mixed.

- News subject country: United States 338, United Kingdom 122, Canada 73, Norway 31 [c1].
- Patent assignee country: US 163, with 32 blank [c1].

the health literature index covers only 219 records, so it is a small, biomedical-leaning sample. The patent counts are limited to title matches. No geography filter was applied (geo was empty).

## Evidence

- [r2] 2024, Earth-Science Reviews, review. Claim: trapping mechanisms and monitoring for geological storage.

- [r2] Massarweh & Abushaikha, 2024, *Earth-Science Reviews*, review. Supports coverage of geological trapping and monitoring. DOI: 10.1016/j.earscirev.2024.104793.
- [r4] Ababou et al., 2018, *Global NEST Journal*, review. Supports mineral carbonation as a reviewed sequestration pathway. DOI: 10.30955/gnj.002597.
- [r7] Benson & Cole, 2008, *Elements*, article. Supports the historical scale estimate quoted above. DOI: 10.2113/gselements.4.5.325.

Prism’s key-number excerpt states: “a billion metric tons or more must be sequestered annually” [r7]. This is a historical statement from the cited article, not a current measured requirement.

## Method and limits

The brief reports typed research for 2017–2025 and additional readable-paper, the health literature index, news, patent, and preprint lanes over their stated windows [c1]. The news trend call covers monthly mentions from 2024-06-01 through 2026-05-01; its exclusive end is 2026-06-01, with newest data censored there due to ingestion lag [c2]. Relative to today, 2026-10-23, the news cutoff is 144 days earlier [c2]. Prism reports table reachability and historical row floors, not proof that every eligible record was ingested [c1][c2].

Counts are records matched to the subject and lane, not unique facilities, tonnes captured, storage volumes, or verified outcomes. The news call uses mention matching; its sentiment-like fields and “critical” classifications are corpus labels, not direct measures of public opinion or scientific validity [c2]. Positive/negative counts may overlap, so they should not be summed as exclusive categories [c2]. The selected evidence and interpretation here do not establish current commercial economics or net climate impact.
